claim_verdicts.evidence: git-commit(1) OPTIONS: "-a / --all: Automatically stage files that have been modified and deleted, but new files you have not told Git about are not affected." Matches the lesson's "--all stages every change to files Git already keeps, with no git add"; untracked files are excluded, and the lesson's phrasing ("files Git already keeps") says exactly that.

git-log(1) OPTIONS: "--oneline: This is a shorthand for --pretty=oneline --abbrev-commit used together." PRETTY FORMATS: "oneline: <hash> <title-line> — This is designed to be as compact as possible." Abbreviated id plus the message's first line, one line per commit.

git-add(1): "-p/--patch: Interactively choose hunks of patch between the index and the work tree and add them to the index." The glossary has no "hunk" entry. A hunk is not only the changed lines: git-diff(1) -U<n> says "The number of context lines defaults to diff.context or 3 if the configuration variable is unset", so a hunk also carries the unchanged lines around them — which is precisely why the edits on lines 3 and 14 fall into two hunks and two edits five lines apart would not. Captured run shows "@@ -1,6 +1,6 @@" and "(1/2) Stage this hunk".
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: A hunk is a block of changed lines together with the unchanged lines Git prints around them (three by default), introduced in `git diff` output by a line starting `@@`; it is the unit `git add --patch` offers for staging.

claim_verdicts.evidence: git-revert(1) DESCRIPTION: "Given one or more existing commits, revert the changes that the related patches introduce, and record some new commits that record them." And: "Usually the command automatically creates some commits with commit log messages stating which commits were reverted." New commits are recorded; the target stays. (The doc's -m/--mainline caveat applies only to merge commits, which this lesson never uses.)

git-bisect(1) DESCRIPTION: "This command uses a binary search algorithm to find which commit in your project's history introduced a bug." And: "Then git bisect picks a commit between those two endpoints and asks you whether the selected commit is 'good' or 'bad'. It continues narrowing down the range until it finds the exact commit that introduced the change."

git-add(1) INTERACTIVE MODE, patch: "it presents the diff between the index and the working tree file and asks you if you want to stage the change of each hunk." git-reset(1) EXAMPLES: "This will ask you about each diff hunk in sequence and you can use simple commands such as 'yes, include this', 'No don't include this'." Captured run confirms: after "y" then "n", git diff --cached holds only the first hunk and git diff still holds the second.
git-blame(1) DESCRIPTION, first sentence: "Annotates each line in the given file with information from the revision which last modified the line."

git-commit(1) DISCUSSION: "Though not required, it's a good idea to begin the commit message with a single short (no more than 50 characters) line summarizing the change, followed by a blank line and then a more thorough description." The wording is "no more than 50 characters", exactly as the lesson states it.

Same DISCUSSION paragraph opens "Though not required, it's a good idea to begin the commit message with…", i.e. Git itself states the shape is a convention. No option in git-commit(1) OPTIONS imposes a subject length or a blank second line; --cleanup only strips comments and whitespace. The lesson's "checks none of that shape when you commit" is supported.

Nếu bạn phải viết "và" ở dòng đầu, đó là hai commit." The lesson's code block matches these six lines character-for-character.

claim_verdicts.evidence: git-switch(1): "-c <new-branch>, --create <new-branch>: Create a new branch named <new-branch> starting at <start-point> before switching to the branch." <start-point>: "The starting point for the new branch. Specifying a <start-point> allows you to create a branch based on some other point in history than where HEAD currently points." "-q, --quiet: Quiet, suppress feedback messages." So `git switch --quiet -c staging-demo main` creates staging-demo at main and switches to it.

git-diff(1), `git diff --cached`: "This form is to view the changes you staged for the next commit relative to the named <commit>… --staged is a synonym of --cached." gitglossary(7): "working tree: The tree of actual checked out files. So "working tree" is Git's own name for the directory the lesson calls the working directory.

claim_verdicts.evidence: git-reset(1) EXAMPLES, "Split a commit apart into a sequence of commits": "You can use git reset to rewind history without changing the contents of your local files, and then successively use git add -p to interactively select which hunks to include into each commit, using git commit -c to pre-populate the commit message." The documented procedure is undo-then-restage; the docs offer no command that splits a commit in place.

issues.quote: on lines 3 and 14 of `README.md` — far enough apart to be two separate blocks of changed lines, which is why `--patch` has two hunks to offer
issues.text: Unlisted claim: "far enough apart" asserts a threshold that depends on a number nothing in the lesson or in .meta.json states. Two changed lines land in separate hunks only when more unchanged lines separate them than Git's context setting — git-diff(1) -U<n>: "The number of context lines defaults to diff.context or 3 if the configuration variable is unset." Edits on lines 3 and 9 would give one hunk and the demonstration would collapse, so the reader gets a rule with its condition removed. No ledger claim covers it (claim 3 defines a hunk, claim 17 only counts @@ lines).
issues.fix: Add a claim to .meta.json (kind `number`, version_key `git`, source git-diff(1) -U<n>) and reword the sentence to name the number, e.g. "— eleven lines apart, more than the three unchanged lines Git prints around a change by default, so they fall into two separate hunks, which is why `--patch` has two to offer".

issues.quote: Each contiguous block of those lines inside one file is a hunk
issues.text: The definition drops the context lines. A hunk is the changed lines plus the unchanged lines Git prints around them (three by default, git-diff(1) -U<n>), which is why a hunk's `@@` header covers more lines than were changed — in the captured output the first hunk is `@@ -1,6 +1,6 @@`, six lines, for one changed line. Defined as "contiguous block of changed lines", the reader cannot predict when two edits share a hunk.
issues.fix: Rewrite the bullet as: "Each block of those lines, together with the few unchanged lines Git prints around it, is a hunk, marked in the output by a line starting `@@`, and the hunk is the unit `git add --patch` offers you one at a time." Update claim 3 in .meta.json to match.

issues.quote: A reviewer, too, reads your change one commit at a time, so the split you choose decides what can be judged in one go.
issues.text: Stated as a universal fact about reviewers, with no condition and no attribution. Claim 23 in .meta.json concedes it is the example repository's position (docs/git/commit-message-examples.md L41: "Người review đọc theo từng commit") plus the lesson's own inference; the prose hides both. Reviewing a change as one combined diff is at least as common, and the lesson offers the reader no way to tell which it is.
issues.fix: Attribute and condition it: "The same file adds a reviewer to that list: when a reviewer goes through your change commit by commit, the split you choose decides what can be judged in one go."

issues.quote: Some teams also require a prefix on the subject line, a category word and a colon, under the name Conventional Commits
issues.text: Unverifiable from the sources this project allows: conventionalcommits.org is not a `docs` root in content/versions.yaml and git-scm.com/docs never names the convention, so the description of what it requires ("a category word and a colon") cannot be checked at the pinned Git version. Claim 12 is therefore `unverified`. The second half is fine — `git grep -ril conventional` at tag stage-0 returns nothing.
issues.fix: Drop the format description and keep only what the repository settles: "Some teams also require a fixed prefix on the subject line; this repository does not, and the four rules stand without it." Then mark claim 12 as a repo fact, or add conventionalcommits.org to content/versions.yaml `standards` if the owner wants the name kept.

issues.quote: `git add --patch README.md` walks the file hunk by hunk and asks about each one, so the two edits reach the staging area separately even though they live in the same file.
issues.text: Read on its own this says any two edits in one file can be separated. The condition arrives only a section later ("far enough apart to be two separate blocks of changed lines"). Section 4 is where I build my picture of the command, and the picture I built there was wrong until section 5 corrected it.
issues.fix: Add the condition where the mechanism is first stated: "…walks the file hunk by hunk — two edits far enough apart are two hunks — and asks about each one, so…".

issues.quote: sed -i '3s|.*|A tiny script that adds up a price list. Work in progress.|' README.md

The prose says what each does ("The two `sed` lines then make the two edits", "The `printf` feeds two answers", "makes a new branch `staging-demo` starting from `main`"), so I was not stuck, but I cannot read the lines themselves: nothing says `3s|.*|…|` means "replace line 3 with this text", so I could not change the demo or tell a typo from the syntax.

issues.quote: The first line makes a new branch `staging-demo` starting from `main`, so the demo edits stay off the main line of history.
issues.text: The paragraph after the script carries seven things: the new branch, the two edits, why lines 3 and 14 give two hunks, the arithmetic of `--stat`, what `printf` does, what the last two commands prove, and that "working tree" is the working directory. I read it twice and still went back for the `--stat` sentence.

issues.quote: The commit holds both edits, because `git commit` takes whatever has changed in a file Git already keeps.
issues.text: Rejecting this option turns on a plain `git commit` staging nothing by itself, and the only place `--all` is explained is a mid-sentence aside back in the situation. The question points me at section 5, where the nearest sentence is "Commit at that moment and the first change is a commit by itself". I got the answer, but by scrolling back to section 2, not from the section the question names.
issues.fix: In section 5, after "Commit at that moment and the first change is a commit by itself", add "— a plain `git commit` writes what the staging area holds and nothing else".

issues.quote: Splitting now means rebuilding from a weeks-old diff the reasoning you no longer hold.
issues.text: This is the third "Beginners often think" bullet reworded ("tidying later means reading a diff you no longer remember and inventing the reasoning after the fact"). I picked it by recognising the wording of a sentence I had just read, and I would have picked it as fast without understanding why splitting early is cheaper.
